prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Sometimes, mystified by the behaviorof one of my sons, my wife will point out if it’s age-appropriate, making me wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on tv and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son,with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn’t yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, or get angry with a friend who told me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No,I read Montaigne who said self-revelation is the purpose of discourse, which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law. Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne says,threw so many hanged Protestantsdown a well you could reach in and touch the top one’s head. Yes,Monluc, who was fond of saying “When the scaffolds are full, use trees,” knew what was appropriate. On occasion I’ll run into a lobbyto avoid greeting a friend, not because my mind vanishes and I can’t remember his name, which is true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when evicted from a strange lobby into a stranger street, where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy,it’s good to know, even momentarily, how to live, among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Sometimes, Last, Montaigne

outputs.L1:
Sometimes, mystified by one of my sons' behavior, my wife will point out whether it's age-appropriate—which makes me wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on TV and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son, with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn't yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, nor did I grow angry with a friend who suggested I soak it in bourbon and garlic. Instead, I read Montaigne, who claimed that self-revelation is the true purpose of discourse—which, in his day, meant knowing whether to feel flattered if a friend dispensed with a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping upon an in-law. Blaise Monluc, the king's lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne tells us, once threw so many hanged Protestants down a well that you could reach in and touch the crown of the topmost head. Yes, Monluc—fond of declaring, "When the scaffolds are full, use trees"—understood what was appropriate.

On occasion, I'll duck into a lobby to avoid greeting a friend, not because my mind has gone blank and I can't recall his name, though that's often true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when cast out of some strange lobby into a stranger street, where every scaffold stands full and bodies sway in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon—without context, explanation, or sympathy—it is good to know, if only for a moment, how to live among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.
outputs.L2:
Every so often, when I'm baffled by something one of my sons has done, my wife will remind me that it's simply typical for his age—which leaves me questioning why, at my age, I still holler at baseball players through the television screen and debate with people long deceased. Just this past week, an errant throw from my eldest son transformed my left ankle into something resembling a swollen eggplant. Rather than losing my temper at the doctors who denied my insurance claim, or snapping at a friend who suggested a bourbon-and-garlic soak, I instead turned to Montaigne. He believed that discourse exists fundamentally to reveal ourselves—though in his era, that self-revelation involved deciding whether one should feel honored if a friend skipped hiring a food-taster, or find humor in a witch cursing an in-law with perpetual tears.

Montaigne recounts how Blaise Monluc, serving as the king's lieutenant general during the civil conflicts, once tossed so many executed Protestants into a well that their bodies stacked high enough for someone to reach down and touch the topmost head. Indeed, Monluc—who famously remarked, "When the scaffolds are full, use trees"—understood exactly what circumstances demanded.

There are moments when I'll duck into a building lobby specifically to dodge an acquaintance, and it isn't because my memory fails me and his name slips away, though that happens too—it's that I need to escape the shadows within myself. Put differently: when you're pushed from an unfamiliar lobby into an equally unfamiliar street, where every gallows stands occupied and figures sway in the melancholy blue stretch of afternoon light, absent any context, justification, or compassion, it becomes valuable to grasp, if only fleetingly, how one might carry on—surrounded by those who are engaged, those consumed by feeling, and those simply lost.
outputs.L3:
My wife has a habit of noting, with the mild anthropological interest of someone cataloguing a species, when our sons behave in ways appropriate to their age. A four-year-old refusing to share a toy: age-appropriate. A seven-year-old melting down over a broken cookie: age-appropriate. She says this not as an excuse but as a kind of calm, scientific observation, and I've come to admire the equanimity behind it. It has, inevitably, turned into a mirror. If a four-year-old's stubbornness is forgivable because it belongs to his stage of life, what excuse do I have for the things I do that are not remotely appropriate to mine—the shouting, for instance, at grown men on a television screen who cannot hear me, who are merely trying to hit a baseball, and who have no idea that a middle-aged man in his living room is questioning their manhood over a called third strike?

The question took on a sharper edge recently when one of my sons, warming up in the backyard, threw a wild pitch that caught me squarely on the ankle. The pain was considerable, the swelling worse, and I found myself faced with a choice about how to respond—not just to the injury, but to the small comedy of adult indignity that follows it. I could have been short with the doctor who told me, unhelpfully, to stay off it. I could have accepted my friend's confident suggestion that I soak the foot in apple cider vinegar and cayenne pepper, a folk remedy he swore by with the fervor of a man who has never once questioned his own conclusions. Instead, hobbled and irritable, I reached for Montaigne.

This was not an accident. Montaigne is good company for a man newly aware of his own absurdity. He believed, with a conviction that still feels startling, that the entire purpose of writing—of talking, really, of any discourse at all—is self-revelation. We think we are describing the world, or history, or other people, but we are always, in the end, describing ourselves: what we notice, what appalls us, what we find funny, what we're willing to forgive. He illustrates this obliquely, through anecdotes that seem at first to be about other people's cruelty or strangeness, and turn out to be about the shape of his own mind.

Consider the story he tells of Blaise Monluc, the French marshal, who once had a group of Protestants hanged and then, needing the scaffold for other business, had them cut down and stacked out of the way with the brisk efficiency of a man clearing furniture. Monluc is said to have complained, half-jokingly, that he didn't have enough gallows to accommodate everyone he felt deserved one. What Montaigne finds worth recording is not simply the violence—the sixteenth century had violence to spare—but the tone: the ease, the good humor, the total absence of doubt. Monluc knew exactly what was appropriate. He had no confusion at all about how to behave, and that certainty is more disturbing, in its way, than the killing itself. It suggests that the feeling of knowing what's right is no guarantee of anything.

I think about this more than I'd like to admit, because I recognize something of Monluc's ease in my own smaller failures of conscience. Not long ago I saw a friend across a hotel lobby and turned quickly toward the elevators, pretending not to have noticed him. I told myself afterward that I simply hadn't seen him, that it was an honest oversight, but this wasn't true. I saw him clearly. I fled because some private weather system was moving through me that day, some obscure shame or exhaustion I couldn't have explained even if he'd asked, and I did not want to perform normalcy for his benefit. Montaigne would say this is more honest than the lie I told myself about it. He would say that knowing how to live doesn't mean arriving at Monluc's kind of certainty—doesn't mean always having the right anecdote or the correct scaffold count—but rather sitting with the parts of ourselves that resist explanation, that come without context or the comfort of anyone's sympathy, including our own.
outputs.L4:
My ankle has been swollen for six days now, a dull purple bruise spreading like a stain beneath the skin, and I have taken to blaming it for everything. The missed train, the terse email I sent to my sister, the way I snapped at the barista who called my name wrong twice—all of it, I tell myself, traces back to this small, stupid injury. As if pain in one part of the body could justify failures of the whole self. I know this isn't true, and yet I keep making the argument anyway, the way we make arguments we don't quite believe because the alternative is admitting something less comfortable: that the anger was already there, waiting for an excuse.

Last Tuesday I ran into an old colleague at the pharmacy and we stood there for four minutes making conversation so strained it felt almost physical, like trying to bend a stick that doesn't want to bend. She asked about my work and I gave an answer that was technically true but somehow completely false in spirit, and she nodded in a way that told me she knew it too. We parted with the usual promises to get coffee sometime, promises neither of us intends to keep, and I limped home feeling that particular flavor of shame that comes from watching yourself perform a version of politeness that convinces no one.

It was that evening, still irritated with myself, that I went back to Montaigne, as I do when the ordinary texture of life starts to feel like sandpaper. There's a passage in "Of Repentance" where he says he has never seen a greater monster or miracle than himself—that in trying to describe himself he has ended up describing all of human nature, its contradictions and cowardices and small vanities. I find this oddly comforting, the way you might find comfort in learning that someone four hundred years dead once also snapped at strangers for no good reason and then spent an evening turning the incident over like a stone, looking for the insect underneath.

What struck me this time, though, wasn't the self-portraiture but something darker running alongside it—his account of Monluc, the military commander whose memoirs Montaigne read with a kind of horrified fascination. Monluc butchered his way through the French Wars of Religion and then, in his old age, sat down to write about it with the satisfaction of a man recounting a well-played hand of cards. Montaigne doesn't excuse this. He holds it up like a specimen, this capacity for a man to commit atrocities and then narrate them without apparent torment, and he asks, implicitly, what separates this monstrousness from the everyday monstrousness we all carry in smaller doses—the impatience, the cruelty we permit ourselves toward waiters and siblings and ourselves, the violence we don't call violence because it never draws blood.

I think about this while nursing my ankle, which suddenly seems like a rather small complaint against the scale of what history actually contains. And yet Montaigne would say—does say, actually, on nearly every page—that the smallness of the complaint is exactly the point. He didn't write about kings and massacres to make his own kidney stones and moods seem trivial by comparison; he wrote about both because he suspected they came from the same source, that the same untidy self capable of writing a testy letter is, under different pressures and different centuries, capable of ordering a slaughter. The gap between Monluc and myself is not a gap in kind but in circumstance, in the accidents of what history hands us to do.

This is not a comfortable thought, but it is, I think, a useful one. It suggests that the work of watching ourselves—really watching, the way Montaigne watched himself with that mixture of affection and unsparing honesty—isn't merely a private hobby for the self-absorbed. It's closer to maintenance. You check the anger the way you check a fence line, not because you expect a wolf every day but because you know that on the day the wolf comes, you'll be glad you looked.

I don't think literature fixes anything. My ankle will heal on its own schedule, indifferent to any essay I read about it. The awkwardness with my former colleague will probably repeat itself the next time we cross paths, because neither of us has done the harder work of admitting we've drifted apart. And my anger, when it comes again—as it will, probably at something equally small—will not be talked down by a four-hundred-year-old Frenchman's wisdom in any permanent sense. But there is something in the act of reading Montaigne, of watching him watch himself and watch Monluc and watch the whole tangled business of being human, that offers a kind of momentary clarity. Not a solution. A flashlight, maybe, held briefly over the mess, just long enough to see the shape of what's actually there before the dark closes back in.

Perhaps that's all we can ask of these old books: not that they solve us, but that they keep us company in the confusion, and remind us, gently and without excuse, that we are not the first to have to figure out what to do with our own capacity for smallness and cruelty, nor will we be the last. The ankle will heal. The shame over the pharmacy conversation will fade into the general sediment of forgotten embarrassments. And somewhere in the back of the mind, filed next to all this, a sentence from an old man in a tower in France will sit quietly, waiting to be useful again the next time the anger rises and I need, if only for a moment, to recognize it before it recognizes me.
outputs.L5:
# On Endings and Reflection

Sometimes the most profound truths arrive not through grand declarations but through quiet, unassuming observations—the kind that Michel de Montaigne mastered in his essays four centuries ago. He understood that wisdom often emerges sideways, through digression and doubt rather than certainty.

Montaigne wrote his essays as a kind of ongoing conversation with himself, revising and adding to them until his last days. He famously kept working on his *Essays* throughout his life, treating the text less as a finished monument and more as a living record of a mind in motion. "I speak to my paper as I speak to the first person I meet," he once noted—a confession that reveals how little he cared for polish over honesty.

Sometimes we forget that his famous question, "Que sais-je?" ("What do I know?"), was not a rhetorical flourish but a genuine posture of humility. In an age of dogmatism and religious violence, Montaigne chose uncertainty as a form of integrity. He distrusted those who claimed final answers, understanding that the last word on any subject is rarely, if ever, truly spoken.

There is something quietly radical in this. Montaigne's essays don't build toward a triumphant conclusion; they circle, digress, contradict themselves, and remain open. In this way, he modeled a kind of thinking that feels remarkably contemporary—skeptical, self-aware, resistant to easy closure.

Perhaps this is why readers return to him across centuries. Sometimes the last lesson a great thinker offers isn't a solution but a method: the courage to sit with not knowing, to examine oneself honestly, and to accept that the essay—like the self—is never truly finished, only set down for now.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem that blends a personal family anecdote with reflections on Montaigne's essays and historical violence.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Reading Montaigne While My Grandmother Tells the Story of the Flood Again

She tells it the same way each time,
as if repetition were a kind of anchor—
how the water came up through the floorboards
in '54, how her mother wrapped the good silver
in a tablecloth and climbed to the roof
with it clutched like a child.
I have heard this story enough times
to know which parts she embellishes,
which parts she has begun, lately, to forget.

*Que sçay-je?* Montaigne asked, folded into his tower,
plague loose in Bordeaux, the wars of religion
turning neighbor against neighbor
with a viciousness that still she cannot fathom, my grandmother,
who thinks the worst thing people do
is what water does—indifferent, rising.

But I have been reading the *Essays* at night
after she goes to bed, and I keep thinking
of the massacre he almost mentions,
sideways, the way you'd mention a scar—
how he watched his countrymen become
unrecognizable to each other,
how he retreated not from cowardice
but from some private understanding
that the self is the only country
you can govern honestly.

My grandmother's silver did not survive the flood.
The water took the tablecloth first,
unraveled her mother's grip finger by finger,
the way history takes the specific
and leaves only the shape of loss behind it.

*I do not portray being, I portray passing,* he wrote.
Not the fixed thing but the weather of the self,
the way a person moves through fear
and comes out the other side
still telling the same story,
polishing it like something recovered
from water, like something saved.

I think of Vassy, of the churches burning,
of Saint Bartholomew's blood in the gutters
while a man in a tower wrote about his cat,
about his kidney stones, about the impossibility
of knowing anything except the shape
of his own uncertain thinking—
and I do not think this was evasion.

I think some part of loving the world
means learning to hold the flood and the essay
in the same two hands,
the burning church and the ordinary Tuesday
when your grandmother, decades on,
still lifts an invisible tablecloth
to the retreating water,
still saves what cannot be saved,
still tells you how the light looked
on the surface of that violence,
so bright, she says, you would have thought
it was something beautiful arriving,
not something come to take
the ground out from under everything you knew.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemplative poem about fatherhood, aging, and self-awareness, weaving in references to Renaissance history.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Medici Gold

I think of Cosimo, old and shrewd,
who built his bank on Florence's need,
then in his final years confessed
that gold could not construct a soul—
only watch one, patient, as it grows
or withers in another's keeping.

My daughter asks me why the moon
follows the car on midnight drives.
I don't know how to tell her yet
that I am the moon in this equation—
fixed, but seeming still to move,
old light arriving late to young eyes.

Lorenzo wrote his poems in the margins
of ledgers, torn between the beautiful
and the necessary, and I understand him now
in ways I couldn't at twenty-five,
when I thought wisdom was a fortress
rather than a slow erosion into use.

I catch my face in windows sometimes—
my father's jaw, his father's tired eyes,
a fresco painted over, layer on layer,
each generation's plaster thinning
till the ghost beneath shows through
and I become the palimpsest I feared.

The Medici built chapels to outlast
their bodies, hedged their bets with stone
against oblivion's slow tide.
I build instead these small rituals—
the bedtime stories, half-remembered rhymes,
hoping some of it will calcify to love

not as monument but as inheritance,
the way Botticelli's Venus still
emerges from her shell each time
we look, not because she's fixed
but because someone kept looking,
kept the seeing alive across the centuries.

I am not wise. I am only older
than I was, still learning what
the fifteenth century already knew:
that power fades, that patronage
is just another word for hope,
that all our chapels crumble eventually—

but the frescoes, if we're careful,
if we tend the plaster right,
might outlast the hands that made them,
might catch some other eye
some other quiet morning,
and for a moment, hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that starts with a domestic scene (a wife commenting on a son's behavior) and spirals into philosophical musings on self-revelation, citing Montaigne.
counterfactuals.output:
**On Confession**

My wife says, *He's doing that thing again,
that squint he does when he's about to lie*—
our son, seven, caught mid-fib about the cookie,
his face already betraying him
before his mouth can catch up.

She knows him that well. Reads him
like weather coming in, the light
going strange before the rain.

And I sit here thinking: how strange
that we can be so legible to one another
and still such riddles to ourselves,
still stumbling around
in the dim rooms of our own motives
like a man who's lost his glasses
groping the nightstand.

Montaigne knew this—
spent twenty years writing himself down,
essay after essay, saying *I am myself
the matter of my book*, as if the self
were a country he could map
by walking it long enough, closely enough,
noting every crooked path and dead end,
every contradiction standing there
plain as a fencepost.

*I cannot fix my object,* he wrote.
*It goes so unsteadily and with such
a natural drunkenness.* And I think
of my son's face, how it gives him away
so easily, so early—
before he's learned the deeper trick
of hiding even from himself,
of building rooms inside the house
he then forgets are there.

My wife laughs at his squint again.
He's protesting now, indignant,
sure of his own innocence—
and maybe that's the saddest part,
or the most human:
that we believe ourselves
even as we're lying,
that the face gives out the secret
the mind hasn't yet admitted knowing.

Montaigne again: *Everyone rushes elsewhere
and into the future, because no one
has arrived at himself.*

I watch my son. I watch myself
watching my son, this endless doubling,
this hall of mirrors we call reflection—
and wonder what my own face does
when I am lying to myself,
what tell I have that I can't see,
what my wife has noticed
in fifteen years of marriage
that I still don't know I do.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem mixing everyday injury and doctor visits with meditations on historical cruelty (like Blaise Monluc) and what it means to live appropriately.
counterfactuals.output:
# Field Notes on the Body's Politics

The gash came from nothing—a cabinet corner,
the careless architecture of my own kitchen—
and the doctor's hands, gloved and competent,
asked nothing of my character while she worked,
only the simple physics of tissue, how deep,
how wide, what the thread must accomplish.

I lay there thinking of Monluc, who wrote
his *Commentaries* like a man confessing
to a God he wasn't sure was listening,
who hanged men from trees for the crime
of being in his century's wrong location,
who called it necessity, called it the age's grammar—

and I wonder what it means to live appropriately
when appropriateness has always been
a border drawn in someone else's blood,
when the same hand that stitches now
might once have held the rope, believing
itself reasonable, believing itself required.

The nurse asks about my tetanus shot.
Five years, I say, maybe six.
Such small maintenances we perform
against the ordinary violence of rust and dirt,
while elsewhere, history keeps its books
in a different ledger, counts its cruelties

as if they were also just maintenance,
just the wound-care of empire, the tetanus
of ideology boostered generation to generation.
Monluc believed he served an order
larger than his conscience—as if conscience
were a luxury, like healing, like this clean room

with its paper gown, its careful anesthetic,
its assumption that pain should be minimized,
that a person matters enough to numb.
Four hundred years ago my cut would have festered
or been cauterized with fire and prayer,
and someone's captain would have called that mercy too.

What does it mean to live appropriately?
Not to feel the weight of every century's dead
with equal grief—that would be its own numbness—
but to notice how the stitches in my arm
are a small argument against the larger silence,
how the doctor's ordinary competence

is a kind of ethics I don't examine enough:
she does not ask if I deserve repair.
The body, in its small emergencies,
keeps teaching me what history forgets—
that cruelty requires a story first,
some frame that makes the wound seem necessary,

while care requires only presence,
only hands that do the unglamorous work
of closing what has opened,
without asking the wound to justify itself,
without deciding first who's earned
the dignity of being mended.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an introspective, essayistic poem in the style of someone influenced by Montaigne, exploring anger, avoidance, and the search for meaning in ordinary life.
counterfactuals.output:
# Of Anger, and the Small Weather of the Self

I.

I have noticed that my anger arrives
like weather I refuse to name—
a pressure in the jaw, a door
closed slightly harder than required—
and I call it *tiredness*, or *the traffic*,
or the failure of some stranger
to perform his small part in my comfort.

This is a lie I tell so gently
I forget that I am lying.

Montaigne, old friend across the centuries,
you sat with your own turbulence
and did not flinch from cataloguing it—
the way a man might catalogue his orchard,
naming each sour apple by its flaw.
I have less courage. I prefer
to let the fruit rot namelessly in grass.

II.

What is avoidance but a kind of prayer—
please, let this feeling pass
before I have to hold it,
before I have to say: *I am afraid*,
*I am ashamed*, *I have been unkind
in ways too small to constitute a story
but large enough to constitute a life.*

We build our days from small evasions.
The unanswered letter. The joke
that lands wrong and is left to lie
where it fell, unaddressed, unmourned.
The way I did not call my father
on the one day that would have mattered,
and told myself the reasons
were about time, were about work,
were anything but what they were:
a small, persistent cowardice
dressed in the clothes of circumstance.

III.

And yet—here is the strange thing—
meaning does not arrive
in the confrontation I keep avoiding.
It comes instead in this:
the smell of coffee at 6 a.m.,
the particular blue of a dish towel
my grandmother once owned,
the way light falls through a window
onto a floor that needs sweeping.

Montaigine, you knew this too—
that the examined life is not a court
where we try ourselves for verdicts,
but a garden where we notice,
day after unremarkable day,
which plants have thrived
and which have quietly died
from want of water we forgot to give.

IV.

So here is what I've come to, walking
this ordinary Tuesday, my anger
folded small inside my coat pocket
like a letter I have not yet opened:
that the self is not a fortress
to be defended, but a house
with many unswept rooms,
and wisdom is not the absence of the mess
but the willingness to enter it,
one room at a time, without apology,
saying: *yes, this too. This also is mine.*

The anger. The avoidance. The strange grace
of loving my own imperfect weather—
not fixing it, not fleeing it,
but sitting with it at the window,
watching how the light still finds a way
to fall, unbothered, on the ordinary floor.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
